Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me

I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home

Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: A needles/medical visual trigger is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is clear trauma-related medical treatment, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in threat, memory, appraisals, or strategies. The rest of the profile centers on interpersonal danger and intrusion rather than medical trauma cues, so this trigger appears clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event
issues.explanation: 'Avoid site of the event' is difficult to interpret coherently for ongoing or domestic partner abuse in this profile. If the abuse occurred in shared/home spaces, the profile would usually show corresponding location-specific triggers or avoidance themes; instead the threat items focus on general vigilance and home intrusion, making this item feel insufficiently anchored to the rest of the selected content.

vignette:
Niran is a 24-year-old painter who came to treatment months after the end of an abusive relationship with a male partner who had become increasingly controlling and violent in the small apartment they once shared. He described one night in particular when an argument turned physical near the front door. His partner had blocked the exit, watched him closely for any sign he might leave, and kept him pinned in the apartment long enough that the space itself began to feel like a trap. What stayed with Niran was not a clean story from beginning to end but flashes: the look of someone staring him down, the sense of waiting for the next move, the terrible uncertainty while seconds stretched and he did not know what would happen next. Those details help explain why, now, the feeling of being watched, moments of uncertainty, and sudden unwanted thoughts about the abuse strike him so forcefully in ordinary life.

In the weeks afterward, he tried hard to manage what broke through. As evening came, he would keep himself busy with errands, videos, or scrolling on his phone because bedtime felt dangerous; he had learned that quiet, dark stretches of the day were when dreams came closest. He also went out of his way to avoid anything that reminded him of his former partner, taking different streets to his studio and refusing invitations to neighborhoods they used to visit together. Over time, those precautions made reminders harder to escape rather than less frequent: the longer route to work, the places he would not enter, and the nightly effort to outrun sleep turned more and more of his day into markers of the abuse itself. When something startled him or felt even vaguely confrontational, he found himself going completely still, the same way he had during the abuse. These habits made sense to him as protection, especially when an unwanted thought or the sense that someone was observing him suddenly flared.

The same triggers also kept his body on alert. At work, if a client was late unlocking a building or a supervisor took too long to answer a text, Niran immediately assumed something bad was happening. Entering galleries, apartment lobbies, or supply stores, he scanned for exits before he could focus on paint colors or the wall in front of him. At home he listened for sounds near the door, straining to catch any sign that someone might be coming in. The feeling of uncertainty was especially potent; any delay seemed loaded with threat, and the sense of being watched made enclosed places feel unsafe. Living at that pitch of danger, he found the world had become crowded with reminders he could not filter out; once his body was already braced, small ambiguities registered immediately as signs connected to what had happened.

His memories remained disjointed and vivid in a way he found hard to explain. Some moments of the abuse were painfully clear—the stance by the door, the stare, the suspended instant before he knew what would happen—while other stretches were blank. He could not put the sequence in order, and when an image did come, he did not experience it as a past event but as if it were happening again right now. The unwanted thoughts did not stay abstract for long; they tipped into reliving, and that reliving made him even more certain he had to stay on guard.

Over time, the way he understood the abuse darkened. Because he had frozen and because he had stayed in the relationship as long as he did, Niran had come to believe the violence said something essential about him: that it happened because of the kind of person he was, that he was inadequate, that he no longer really belonged anywhere. Once he saw himself and the world that way, ordinary moments caught on those meanings much more easily; a pause at a doorway, a stranger's glance, or a text left unanswered no longer stayed neutral for long but quickly became the kind of cue that pulled him back toward the abuse. Those beliefs sharpened his sensitivity to other people’s attention. If someone glanced at him too long on the train or in a worksite hallway, he felt exposed at once, as though others could see the weakness he despised in himself. Once that feeling took hold, he watched doors, listened for entry sounds, and braced for harm more intensely.

The cycle tightened through his efforts to cope. Avoiding reminders of his ex narrowed his world and left the memories less tested by ordinary life; they returned in abrupt, fragmented bursts that felt current rather than finished. Staying up to avoid dreams meant he was exhausted, and in that tired state he was more easily flooded by unwanted thoughts at work. Freezing whenever he felt threatened left him ashamed afterward, which fed his sense of inadequacy and made future moments of uncertainty even more charged. The more he scanned for exits and listened for danger, the more often he noticed signs that seemed to confirm he was not safe, and those cues pulled up the same broken pieces of memory again.

By the time he sought help, the effects had become visible in his daily life. He was missing deadlines on painting jobs because he lost time checking entrances and waiting for his body to settle, and his partner now found him distant and unreachable at night, when he would resist going to bed and tense at every noise in the apartment. Niran came in frightened by how quickly a delay, a look, or an unwanted thought could make the past feel present. More than anything, he feared that this constant vigilance meant he had been permanently changed into someone weak and out of place; at the same time, he still hoped treatment might help him sleep, work, and feel that his life belongs to him again.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows negative beliefs increasing vigilance and sensitivity, but it does not clearly state that negative appraisals themselves lead to trauma reminders or triggering cues.
The vignette conveys that threat leads to vigilance and memory reliving, but it does not explicitly show the sense of threat causing triggers or reminders to arise.
The vignette shows avoidance and scanning strengthening memory, appraisals, and threat, but it does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies generate or increase triggers/reminders.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette shows negative beliefs increasing vigilance and sensitivity, but it does not clearly state that negative appraisals themselves lead to trauma reminders or triggering cues.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette conveys that threat leads to vigilance and memory reliving, but it does not explicitly show the sense of threat causing triggers or reminders to arise.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette shows avoidance and scanning strengthening memory, appraisals, and threat, but it does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies generate or increase triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
